config.title: Viewport units (vw, vh, vmin, vmax)

intro.title: Viewport units (vw, vh, vmin, vmax)
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a responsive webpage layout that adapts to the size of the browser window. You will learn the core concept of viewport units, which are CSS length units relative to the browser's viewport size. The main technologies involved are the CSS units vw (viewport width), vh (viewport height), vmin (viewport minimum), and vmax (viewport maximum). You will use these units to size elements like headers, sections, and images proportionally to the screen. By the end, you'll understand how to create flexible designs that work on different screen sizes without media queries.
intro.usecase: Viewport units are essential for creating responsive layouts that adapt to any screen size. You'll use vw and vh to build full-screen hero sections, modals, and landing pages that fill the entire browser window. Designers rely on vmin and vmax to ensure UI elements like navigation bars, side panels, and image galleries maintain proper proportions on both mobile and desktop displays. These units are particularly valuable for dashboards, data visualizations, and admin panels where content must dynamically resize across different devices without breaking the layout.

objectives: Apply viewport width (vw) units to create responsive element widths
Implement viewport height (vh) units to control element heights relative to screen size
Configure layouts using vmin units to adapt to the smaller viewport dimension
Construct responsive designs with vmax units based on the larger viewport dimension
Manipulate font sizes using viewport units for scalable typography
Integrate multiple viewport units within a single layout for comprehensive responsiveness
Update existing CSS measurements by replacing fixed units with viewport-relative units

steps.title: Create a CSS file and understand the viewport concept
steps.instruction: Create a new CSS file named 'styles.css' and add a CSS comment at the top explaining that viewport units are relative to the browser window size.
steps.hint: Start by creating a CSS file. Use a CSS comment (/* comment */) to write your explanation about viewport units.
steps.analogousExample:
/* This is a CSS comment explaining a concept */
/* Viewport units like vw and vh are relative to the browser window */
steps.seedCode: /* Add your comment here explaining viewport units */
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS file is created with a comment explaining that viewport units are relative to the browser window size.
successCriteria: The CSS file contains a comment that mentions viewport units and their relation to browser window size.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the CSS file, but your comment doesn't fully explain viewport units. Make sure your comment mentions that viewport units are relative to the browser window size.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS file wasn't created correctly or the comment is missing. Create a CSS file named 'styles.css' and add a comment explaining viewport units are relative to browser window size.

steps.title: Set up basic HTML structure for testing viewport units
steps.instruction: Add a div element with the class 'viewport-demo' to serve as the container for your viewport unit examples.
steps.hint: Create a simple div element with a class attribute. This will be the main container where you'll apply viewport unit styles in later steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS rule for a .viewport-demo class is created, ready to have viewport unit styles applied to it.
successCriteria: The CSS file contains a .viewport-demo selector with an empty rule set.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've created a CSS rule with the selector '.viewport-demo' (including the dot).
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule for the viewport-demo container wasn't found. Create a CSS selector that starts with '.viewport-demo' followed by curly braces.

steps.title: Apply vw (viewport width) unit to an element
steps.instruction: Inside the .viewport-demo selector, set the width property to 50vw.
steps.hint: The vw unit represents a percentage of the viewport width. 50vw means 50% of the viewport width.
steps.expectedOutcome: The .viewport-demo element will now have a width equal to 50% of the viewport width.
successCriteria: The .viewport-demo selector has a width property set to 50vw.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're setting the width property (not height or another property) and using the vw unit.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're adding the width property with 50vw inside the .viewport-demo selector.

steps.title: Apply vh (viewport height) unit to an element
steps.instruction: Add a height property to the .viewport-demo element and set its value to 30vh.
steps.hint: The vh unit sets a dimension relative to the viewport height. Add 'height: 30vh;' inside the .viewport-demo selector.
steps.expectedOutcome: The .viewport-demo element will have a height equal to 30% of the viewport height.
successCriteria: The .viewport-demo selector includes a height property with the value 30vh.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added the height property with exactly '30vh' as the value inside the .viewport-demo selector.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires adding a height property with the value 30vh to the .viewport-demo element. Please try again.

steps.title: Combine vw and vh units on different elements
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule for a class named '.box-vh' that sets its height to 30vh.
steps.hint: Create a new selector starting with .box-vh and inside its curly braces, add a height property with a value using vh units.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a new CSS class that uses viewport height units, allowing you to see how different elements can use different viewport units.
successCriteria: A CSS rule for .box-vh exists with a height property set to 30vh.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've created a CSS rule for .box-vh with a height property using vh units.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires creating a new CSS class named .box-vh with a height property using vh units. Please try again.

steps.title: Apply vmin (viewport minimum) unit to an element
steps.instruction: Create a new CSS rule for a class named '.box-vmin' that sets both width and height to 25vmin.
steps.hint: The vmin unit is based on the smaller dimension of the viewport (width or height). Use the syntax 'width: 25vmin; height: 25vmin;'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new CSS rule that creates an element sized at 25% of the viewport's smaller dimension.
successCriteria: The CSS contains a '.box-vmin' rule with both width and height set to 25vmin.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both width and height are set to 25vmin in the '.box-vmin' rule.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule should define both width and height properties using the vmin unit. Try creating a '.box-vmin' class with 'width: 25vmin; height: 25vmin;'.

steps.title: Compare vmin and vmax behavior with window resizing
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule for a .comparison-container that will hold both vmin and vmax boxes side by side for easy comparison.
steps.hint: Create a new CSS selector starting with .comparison-container and set its display property to flex.
steps.expectedOutcome: A flex container is created that will allow visual comparison of vmin and vmax boxes when they're added later.
successCriteria: The .comparison-container rule exists with display: flex property
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added the .comparison-container selector with display: flex.
steps.feedbackWrong: The comparison container wasn't created correctly. Create a .comparison-container rule with display: flex.

steps.title: Use viewport units for font sizes
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule for a class named '.responsive-text' that sets font-size to 3vw.
steps.hint: Create a new CSS selector that targets elements with class 'responsive-text' and apply the font-size property with a viewport width unit.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new CSS rule will be created that applies responsive font sizing using viewport width units.
successCriteria: The CSS file contains a '.responsive-text' selector with 'font-size: 3vw;' property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the rule, but check that it uses exactly 'font-size: 3vw;' with the correct selector.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule for responsive text using viewport units wasn't created correctly. Try adding '.responsive-text { font-size: 3vw; }'.

steps.title: Create a responsive layout using all viewport units
steps.instruction: Create a new CSS rule for a .responsive-layout class that uses all four viewport units (vw, vh, vmin, vmax) to create a responsive container.
steps.hint: Define a .responsive-layout selector and set properties like width, height, padding, and margin using different viewport units.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new CSS rule that demonstrates practical use of all viewport units together in a layout container.
successCriteria: The .responsive-layout rule exists and contains at least one property using each of the four viewport units (vw, vh, vmin, vmax).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your .responsive-layout rule includes properties using all four viewport units: vw, vh, vmin, and vmax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The .responsive-layout rule is missing or doesn't properly use all four viewport units. Review the instruction and try again.
